content.text: The termination architecture meets the preferred position: Customer has an unrestricted convenience right on 30 days' notice with a prepaid-fee refund, and Vendor has no convenience right at all.

input.quote: 9.4 Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form without cause by delivering the written notice specified in Section 29.4. Customer owes only accrued Fees, and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees for the period after termination.
input.rationale: Section 9.4 gives us a convenience ("without cause") right over the whole Agreement or any individual Order Form, and Section 29.4 fixes that notice period at "thirty days before the effective termination date," delivered by the written methods in Section 29.1 — so the preferred 30-day written-notice standard is satisfied. On exit we owe "only accrued Fees" (no early-termination fee or penalty), and Vendor must "refund prepaid Fees for the period after termination," reinforced by Section 10.2 ("Vendor shall refund prepaid recurring Fees covering the period after termination"), which is a pro-rata refund in substance. Vendor has no convenience right anywhere: its termination rights are limited to uncured material breach (9.1) and insolvency (9.2), while 9.3 adds Customer-only immediate triggers and Section 20.5 expressly bars Vendor from terminating unaffected Services; Section 24.4 also denies Vendor any right to terminate on our change of control. The clause therefore meets the preferred position, not merely the fallback, in a three-year term (8.1). Noted but not flagged under this rule: Section 7.7's late-payment liquidated damages (fifteen percent of annual Fees per week) is a payment-default penalty rather than an early-termination fee, so it is addressed under the payment/liquidated-damages rule rather than here.
